stem: What was the most important consequence of the destruction of the buffalo for the Plains peoples?

stimulus.source_note: Colonel Richard Dodge's 1871 description as quoted in HISTORY.com, "Why Is the Bison America's National Mammal?"; herd figures from the U.S. Geological Survey (about 20-30 million bison before the slaughter, barely more than 1,000 by 1889) and Hornaday's 1889 census count of 1,091.
stimulus.text:
"The whole country appeared one mass of buffalo," wrote Colonel Richard Dodge when he traveled the Santa Fe Trail in 1871.

(Background from the books: between 1871 and 1883, hide hunters working in teams killed millions of bison for their skins, and railroads carried the hides east. When the Smithsonian sent an expedition to Montana in 1886 to collect specimens from the vanishing herds, few remained; Hornaday's 1889 census counted only 1,091 bison left in all of North America.)

options.text: They could no longer feed themselves and depended on government rations on reservations
They became wealthy by selling buffalo bones to fertilizer factories
options.misconception: Background: bone picking earned a few people pennies; it never replaced a way of life or fed whole peoples.

options.text: They moved east and became factory workers in Chicago and New York
options.misconception: Background: the Plains peoples were confined to reservations in the West, not moved east into factories.

options.text: They were given large new reservations with better farmland
options.misconception: Background: reservation lands were typically the least desirable ground, and the Dawes Act then broke even those up.

rationales.A: With the herds gone, the hunting life was gone with them. The peoples who had lived on the buffalo had to live on government rations, confined to reservations.
rationales.B: Background: gathering bones paid almost nothing. It was salvage after a collapse, not a new livelihood.
rationales.C: Background: the Plains peoples stayed in the West, on reservations. No migration to eastern factories followed the slaughter.
rationales.D: Background: the reservations were poor land, and the Dawes Act of 1887 then divided even that. No better farmland was given.
rationales.general:
Kill the food and you kill the freedom that went with it.
1. Remember what the buffalo was: the whole economy of the Plains peoples.
2. Take it away, and ask what is left. Background: no herds to hunt, no way to feed a family on the open Plains.
3. Name the result. Dependence on government rations, on reservations, under government supervision.
Remember: destroying a people's food is a faster conquest than any battle.
